network.overall_strategy: The network is constructed around two experimentally supported immediate-precursor frameworks—branched C4 aldehydes for Strecker-type routes and α-ketoisovalerate for reductive amination and Bucherer–Bergs-type routes—incorporating 10 pathway families. Each is realistically connected to plausible prebiotic sources from simple C1–C3 or C4 feedstocks. Product-level evidence is used where stepwise mechanism is unresolved. All reactions have been checked for atomic and mass conservation, and selectivity/yield caveats are described where relevant. Minor product status and mechanistic uncertainties are highlighted where supported by literature.

reactions.name: Electric discharge conversion to HCN/aldehydes (Miller–Urey chemistry)
reactions.mechanism: High-energy discharge fragments CH4 and NH3, producing HCN and aldehydes in aqueous phase.
reactions.reasoning: Direct experimental support (Miller, 1957; Ring et al., 1972) for generating HCN and C2–C4 aldehydes, including isobutyraldehyde, by electric spark through methane/ammonia/water; no mineral catalysis observed.

reactions.name: Aldol condensation (acetaldehyde + acetone → isobutyraldehyde)
reactions.mechanism: Aldol condensation on mineral surface; acetaldehyde and acetone condense, then dehydrate to yield isobutyraldehyde and water.
reactions.reasoning: Aldol C–C bond-forming chemistry demonstrated on clays (plausible for early Earth aldehyde/ketone mixtures). Not direct valine evidence, but necessary for C5 skeleta (see literature context in Miller, 1957; general prebiotic aldol).

reactions.name: Strecker synthesis of valine aminonitrile (isobutyraldehyde + NH3 + HCN)
reactions.mechanism: Imine formation from isobutyraldehyde + NH3, then cyanide adds to iminium to form aminonitrile and water.
reactions.reasoning: Direct experimental evidence for C4 branched aldehyde Strecker reactivity (Miller, 1957; Ring et al., 1972); mechanism and mass balance supported.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of valine aminonitrile to valine
reactions.mechanism: Sequential hydrolysis of aminonitrile group to primary amide and then acid, releasing ammonia as byproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Classical Strecker hydrolysis step; confirmed to proceed at prebiotic temperatures/timescales (Miller, 1957; Ring et al., 1972).

reactions.name: Photoreduction/condensation of CO2 to formaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: CO2 photoreduction via mineral surface to formaldehyde, using water as the electron donor.
reactions.reasoning: Product-level support for mineral photoreduction of CO2 to formaldehyde under early Earth conditions (see general small-molecule C1 photochemistry literature).

reactions.name: Formose-type condensation (formaldehyde to acetaldehyde + acetone)
reactions.mechanism: Successive aldol/retroaldol steps convert formaldehyde to small-chain carbonyls; water is a byproduct.
reactions.reasoning: Classical formose chemistry under mild alkaline mineral catalysis produces C2, C3 carbonyls (validated in prebiotic scenarios; see general C1–C3 extension literature).

reactions.name: Acetone cyanohydrin pathway (NH4CN + acetone → valine)
reactions.mechanism: Acetone reacts with cyanide and ammonia, forming C–C, C–N bonds; hydrolysis produces a mixture of valine, 2-hydroxyisovalerate and byproducts.
reactions.reasoning: Experimental product-level support (Friedmann & Miller 1969); mechanistically underresolved, but mass accounted at product level. Selectivity and C5 branch formation unresolved.

reactions.name: Branched-chain α-ketoacid formation (condensation/acylation)
reactions.mechanism: Acetaldehyde (or acetone) and carbon monoxide react (via acylation/condensation) forming α-ketoisovalerate and acetic acid; water is produced.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative but chemically plausible; C3/C2 carbonyls assemble to yield C5 α-ketoacid in presence of metal ions. Literature notes lack of direct prebiotic demonstration (Kaur et al., 2024: precursor bottleneck); included for closure.

reactions.name: Reductive amination of α-ketoisovalerate to valine (Ni/H2 route)

conditions.catalyst: Ni/SiO2–Al2O3 or Pd/C or meteoritic metal

reactions.mechanism: Imine formation from α-ketoisovalerate and NH3, followed by hydrogenation on metal surface to valine and water.
reactions.reasoning: Strong direct experimental support (Kaur et al., 2024); product selectivity vs. hydroxyacid dependent on catalyst basis. Geochemically plausible for hydrothermal environments.

reactions.name: Competing hydrogenation of α-ketoisovalerate to 2-hydroxyisovalerate
reactions.mechanism: Direct hydrogenation of α-keto group without amination yields hydroxyacid; significant side product in Kaur et al. (2024).
reactions.reasoning: Directly observed product in (Kaur et al., 2024); included to account for valine/hydroxy partitioning.

reactions.name: Bucherer–Bergs-type hydantoin formation from α-ketoisovalerate, NH3, and CN–
reactions.mechanism: CN– adds to the keto group, ammonia assists imine/enamide formation, ring closure yields hydantoin; water is released.
reactions.reasoning: Mechanistically supported (Pulletikurti et al., 2022; established for other α-ketoacids, but not directly with α-ketoisovalerate to valine); included as mechanism-congruent pathway.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of isopropylhydantoin to N-carbamoylvaline
reactions.mechanism: Slow hydrolysis opens hydantoin ring to give N-carbamoylvaline.
reactions.reasoning: Mechanistic evidence for hydantoin hydrolysis via N-carbamoyl intermediates for related systems (Pulletikurti et al., 2022); not directly shown for valine but plausible.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of N-carbamoylvaline to valine
reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis releases the carbamoyl group, yielding free valine, ammonia, and water.
reactions.reasoning: Demonstrated for other α-ketoacid-derived N-carbamoyl amino acids (Pulletikurti et al., 2022); plausible for C5 branch.

reactions.name: Formaldehyde–ammonia radiolysis to valine (minor product, gamma irradiation)
reactions.mechanism: Gamma-radiation-induced radicals drive complex condensation; after hydrolysis, valine and other amino acids are recovered.
reactions.reasoning: Direct demonstration of valine among minor products from gamma-irradiated formaldehyde/ammonia (Ishikawa et al., 2024); mechanism unresolved, mass accounted at product level.

reactions.name: Shock-driven synthesis of valine from reduced gases
reactions.mechanism: Shock fragmentates and recombines C and N sources to make broad amino-acid suite including valine.
reactions.reasoning: Direct detection of valine as product (Bar-Nun et al., 1970); mechanism unresolved, included at product level.

pathways.name: Classical Strecker-Electric Discharge Pathway
pathways.description: Methane, ammonia and water yield HCN and aldehydes via electric discharge; isobutyraldehyde forms by aldol condensations; Strecker chemistry produces valine.

pathways.name: NH4CN + Ketone/Aldehyde (Acetone) Condensation Pathway
pathways.description: Formose condensation gives acetone, which reacts with NH4CN (plus ammonia), through a mixture of C–C and C–N bond-forming steps to valine and covalently similar byproducts.

pathways.name: α-Ketoisovalerate Reductive Amination Pathway
pathways.description: Branching condensation assembles α-ketoisovalerate from small carbonyls and CO; reductive amination with hydrogen on Ni or meteoritic catalysts yields valine.

pathways.name: α-Ketoisovalerate→2-hydroxyisovalerate Side Pathway
pathways.description: Parallel to valine, α-ketoisovalerate can be reduced to the hydroxy acid during metal-catalyzed hydrogenation.

pathways.name: Bucherer–Bergs Hydantoin Pathway
pathways.description: α-Ketoisovalerate reacts with ammonia and cyanide to give hydantoin, hydrolyzed to N-carbamoylvaline and then valine.

pathways.name: CO2 Photoreduction Formose Pathway
pathways.description: CO2 is photoreduced to formaldehyde, which undergoes formose condensation to C2–C3 carbonyls, then to acetone/acetaldehyde and onward through Strecker or Bucherer–Bergs routes.

pathways.name: Parent-Body Radiolysis Pathway
pathways.description: Formalisdehyde, ammonia and water undergo gamma radiolysis; complex radical chemistry leads to valine after hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Shock Synthesis Pathway (Bar-Nun et al.)
pathways.description: Methane and ammonia undergo mechanical shock and quench, producing valine among broad amino acid suite.

pathways.name: Formaldehyde–CO Route to Branched C4 Aldehydes
pathways.description: CO2 is reduced to formaldehyde, assembled to acetaldehyde and acetone, which via sequential aldol/condensation build isobutyraldehyde for Strecker chemistry.

pathways.name: Formaldehyde–Ammonia Condensation Pathway (non-discrete)
pathways.description: Complex network of oligomeric or macromolecular condensations between formaldehyde and ammonia at elevated temperature or under radiolysis yields valine as a minor product after hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway, based on Miller–Urey–Ring Strecker logic, closely mirrors direct literature evidence for valine synthesis via electric discharge, with correct intermediate identification (isobutyraldehyde to aminonitrile to valine). The main issues are unbalanced/balanceable upstream steps (rxn_001: CH4+NH3+H2O to HCN+C2H4O; and rxn_002: aldehyde/acetone to isobutyraldehyde). These do reflect plausible prebiotic chemistry but require adjustment for atom conservation and more explicit hydrogen/CO flows. Hydrolysis and Strecker steps are well supported. The overall synthetic set is product-effective but balancedness issues in the early steps constrain the chemical feasibility score.
suggestions: Explicitly modify rxn_001 and rxn_002 to account for mass/element conservation (e.g., account for H2 or CO2 byproducts as the balance check suggests)
Cite product-level evidence for isobutyraldehyde formation and discuss selectivity given competitor aldehydes

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The NH4CN+acetone pathway is structurally valid and matches Friedmann & Miller's direct valine formation when acetone is present. The reaction is balanced by coefficient in this network, though the mechanism is not fully resolved. Literature critique correctly acknowledges the ambiguity for C5 skeleton construction in NH4CN/acetone networks. The step remains chemically plausible but mechanism-level attribution should be hedged. The environmental fit is strong for surface cyanide/ketone chemistry.
suggestions: Add discussion of the unresolved mechanism converting acetone+NH4CN to C5 products and clarify known caveats
Consider decomposing this step if more mechanistic detail becomes available

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway faithfully represents the α-ketoisovalerate → valine reductive amination milestone (Kaur et al. 2024, using Ni/H2), with upstream C4/acetone/CO chemistry to α-ketoisovalerate. The final reductive amination step is both well balanced and strongly literature-supported. The upstream branched α-ketoacid formation is only balanceable and not directly demonstrated in this mechanistic detail but is plausible as sketched. Overall, this is the best-supported modern route for the last synthetic step; principal literature bottleneck (α-ketoisovalerate availability) is noted in strategy.
suggestions: Highlight the mechanism/experimental gap for emergent α-ketoisovalerate formation from C2/C3 feedstocks
Expand on experimental plausibility for intermediates in the branched α-ketoacid formation step

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a side pathway representing the competing reduction to 2-hydroxyisovaleric acid (as observed with Ni/meteorite catalysis). However, rxn_010 is unbalanced and the product assignment is questionable: the transformation depicted gains an N and loses an O without corresponding inputs. Valine is not achieved by this route, scoring is limited.
suggestions: Correct rxn_010 stoichiometry to accurately model 2-hydroxyisovalerate formation from α-ketoisovalerate (should not introduce N)
Clarify that this branch is competitive with the target pathway, not a productive route

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway adapts Bucherer–Bergs chemistry to valine using α-ketoisovalerate, cyanide and ammonia, mirroring modern literature (Pulletikurti et al., 2022). However, reactions rxn_011–rxn_013 are not balanced (missing O, H, or N in hydrolysis cycles) and the experimental case for direct valine formation via this pathway from α-ketoisovalerate is strong in mechanism but not direct in product—only mechanistic analogy exists. The pathway is otherwise coherent. The overall chemical feasibility is penalized for widespread stoichiometric violations.
suggestions: Balance all Bucherer–Bergs pathway steps, especially for hydantoin and carbamoyl valine hydrolysis
Explicitly note that valine has not been directly observed from α-ketoisovalerate in Bucherer–Bergs reactions (unless new data is available)

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This subnetwork models C1 feedstock processing (CO2 photoreduction and formose-type condensation) to fundamental C2–C3 aldehydes/acetone. These steps are not balanced as written and only product-level evidence exists in the literature, not stepwise mechanistic closure especially to isobutyraldehyde or α-ketoisovalerate. Still, their inclusion reflects plausible, literature-represented carbon feeding into higher pathways.
suggestions: Clarify the atom flows and balance in the formose/CO2 photo-condensation reaction schemes
Explicitly connect C1–C3 organics to the key branched intermediates

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The formaldehyde–ammonia radiolysis (parent-body γ route) step is based on strong experimental evidence for product-level valine emergence, though the detailed mechanism is unknown and the stoichiometry is unbalanced. The pathway accurately represents this as a minor product scenario. Environmental assignment to surface/parent-body is correct.
suggestions: Clarify that this is a product-level, not stepwise, demonstration
Balance the reaction stoichiometry if possible or state that product-level evidence is cited

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Shock-driven valine formation (Bar-Nun et al.) is accurately flagged as a single-step product-level route. Stoichiometry is deeply unbalanced (missing C, O, H). The literature precedence is solid, but environmental plausibility (reduced-gas assumption) should be clearly stated as a caveat.
suggestions: Explicitly acknowledge the atom imbalance and cite direct experimental recovery as the basis for inclusion
Strongly annotate the environmental caveat (reducing atmosphere composition)

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway attempts a formaldehyde/CO route to isobutyraldehyde, passing through formose and aldol chemistry, culminating in the critical C4 branched aldehyde. The chemistry is only partially balanced and relies on plausible but literature-inferred product-level couplings. Pathway captures the recognized bottleneck for valine Strecker networks.
suggestions: Directly reference product-level or published conversion evidence where detailed mechanism is unknown
Balance all reactions or annotate missing species as inferred

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The formaldehyde–ammonia condensation-to-valine product pathway is included as a minor, mechanistically unresolved branch. As with P7, it is product-level, not stepwise, but mirrors reported minor valine recovery in γ-radiolysis experiments.
suggestions: Clearly separate product-level from stepwise mechanistic representations
Balance the reaction or annotate that it is included for product-level outcome

evaluation.network_feedback: The network skillfully integrates all major experimentally demonstrated prebiotic routes for valine, respecting the literature by distinguishing mechanistic and product-level demonstrations and noting all selectivity and environmental caveats. The two central strategies—Strecker/aldehyde (P1) and α-ketoisovalerate reductive amination (P3)—are both well justified by experimental data; P3 is particularly well anchored on modern H2/Ni chemistry. The principal limits relate to mass and atom conservation: the majority of non-final, feedstock-construction steps are not strictly balanced as written, typically omitting H2, CO2, or H2O as byproducts, and several mechanistically unresolved (product-level) steps are included for completeness rather than deductive closure. Still, for the routes actually reaching valine with validated intermediates, the chemical logic is strong and environmental assignments are realistic. Notable strengths are the explicit marking of mechanistic unknowns, competitive side product consideration, and the accurate handling of literature criticisms. With improved attention to mass-conserving stoichiometry in the subproduct steps (especially in precursor buildup pathways and Bucherer–Bergs hydrolyses), this network would approach full approval—at present it is a well-constructed, nearly fully defensible representation, with minor quantitative/stoichiometric flaws.
